display.purpose: Topmost heading only. Used almost nowhere by design.

headline.purpose: The workhorse section label. Uppercase, 14px, wide-tracked.

title.purpose: The narrowest label tier, for headings inside dense groups.

label.purpose: Control labels and button text. The default reading size.

body.purpose: Counts, dimensions and readouts. Always mono so a value is never read as a name.

shadows.name: raised
shadows.purpose: Short chromatic lift. Default for Button and stage slot.

shadows.name: sunken
shadows.value: inset 0 1px 0 color-mix(in oklab, <tint shadow> 88%, transparent), inset 0 1px 3px color-mix(in oklab, <tint shadow> 16%, transparent)
shadows.purpose: Carved recess for wells and inputs.

shadows.name: flat
shadows.purpose: The neutral default. Every passive surface.

motion.name: ease-bench
motion.purpose: The only easing curve in the system, on every pressable.

motion.name: duration-bench
motion.purpose: Single transition duration, on background-color, border-color, color, box-shadow and transform.

motion.name: press-scale
motion.purpose: The press acknowledgement, applied on :active to every pressable.

narrative.overview:
An optical bench lines up specimens under a single light and lets you turn one adjustment at a time. That is the whole proposition here. This system is not a set of pretty surfaces; it is an instrument for deciding which surface becomes the system's surface. Every choice the design makes serves that one job — making a difference visible, and making it attributable to exactly one variable.

The geometry is deliberately sober. Corners are short (rounded.md, 6px). Borders are hairlines (1px). There are no gradients on any component, no shadows of atmosphere, no decorative motion. Type is two system families at small sizes, with headings set in uppercase and wide-tracked so they read as index tabs rather than titles. All of this restraint exists to protect the one thing the system is actually loud about: color. Eight tinted accents are running at once across a matrix of variants, and every visual decision here is in service of keeping them mutually distinguishable.

The result should feel like precision instrumentation rather than a product: dense, quiet, and completely uninterested in impressing anyone. What earns delight here is not polish on any single component — it is the moment a whole matrix resolves at once and the comparison becomes obvious.
keyCharacteristics: A tint is applied through three independent channels — background, border, shadow — and any subset is legal.
Every accent exists as a light/dark pair whose hue shifts between themes; the dark palette is re-tuned, not merely darkened.
Elevation is a value you choose and compare, a peer of color and fill density, not decoration.
Two fill densities: solid, and a veil at 18% of the tint.
Geometry stays quiet so the palette can be loud.
Interactive controls are minimum 44x44px at the hit level, even when the visible box is far smaller.

rules.name: The Three-Channel Rule
rules.body: A tint reaches a surface through exactly three channels: background, border, shadow. Each is independently switchable, and any subset is legal. Three channels filled means this surface is the color. Border and shadow only means this surface is neutral with an accent. Background only means a wash with no edge. Never reach for a named combination like "accented" or "tinted" — the correct subset is a property of the component, not of the vocabulary.

rules.name: The One-Accent Rule
rules.body: A surface carries at most one tint. Two accents on one surface is a defect, not a style.

rules.name: The Eight Rule
rules.body: Exactly eight tints exist. Adding a ninth means removing one. The count is small enough that all eight can share a screen and stay mutually legible; that property is the reason for the number.

rules.name: The Two-Face Rule
rules.body: Two families, never three. Mono is reserved for measured values; if something is not a measured value, it is sans. A third family has no meaning to add here.

rules.name: The Measured-Value Rule
rules.body: Any string that is a value rather than a name gets mono: the node-count readout, filter option labels that are literal tokens (soft, raised, true), and the variant slug under test. This is what lets the operator scan a matrix and pick out values from names without reading them.

rules.name: The 4px Rule
rules.body: No dimension is a free number. Every gap, pad, offset and radius is a named step of the spacing scale, and every control dimension is a named step of the layout scale.

rules.name: The Stable-Gutter Rule
rules.body: Anything that scrolls reserves its scrollbar space permanently. Reflow caused by a scrollbar appearing is never acceptable in a comparison tool, because it changes the very alignment the operator is reading.

rules.name: The Shadow-Is-A-Variant Rule
rules.body: Shadow is one of the axes a surface is judged along, exactly like color and fill density. A shadow that appears for reasons of hierarchy rather than selection has been applied without permission.

rules.name: The Tinted-Shadow Rule
rules.body: No neutral-black shadow anywhere. Every shadow takes its color from the surface's own tint channel, so that depth and hue never disagree.

rules.name: The 18% Rule
rules.body: Fills, borders and shadows are one density family: veiled fill at 18%, subtle border at 10%, strong border at 20%, raised shadow at 36%. These four numbers are the entire opacity vocabulary of the system.

rules.name: The 6px Rule
rules.body: 6px is the system's corner, and it is not a default to be overridden casually. Larger radii are reserved for genuinely rounded containers; smaller radii are for controls. A component whose corner differs from its role's default needs a reason written next to it.

rules.name: The Hairline Rule
rules.body: One border weight exists. Weight is expressed by opacity and color, never by thickness.

dos: Do judge every variant in all three themes before accepting it. A tint that survives only one color scheme has not been evaluated.
Do set a surface's three channel flags explicitly rather than inheriting them. Card is border + shadow with no fill; Button is all three. The default is not the answer.
Do keep elevation at its role default: Card flat, Button raised, stage slot raised, panel flat.
Do read tint colors through the colors light/dark vars, never from the raw palette ramps. The light-dark() pair is what makes the theme flip correct.
Do keep hit areas at 44px (layout.controlTouchTarget) even when the visible control is 18px.
Do let color carry the expressiveness. If a surface feels flat, change the tint or the elevation — not the geometry.
donts: Don't add a ninth tint without removing one, and don't name new accents with Material or generic scales. The system's names (neutral, aurora, solder, purple, amber, error, aqua, orange) are the vocabulary; the values are light-dark() pairs.
Don't apply two tints to one surface.
Don't introduce a third font family, or use the mono face for anything that is not a measured value.
Don't use a neutral-black shadow, a glow focus ring, or a gradient on any component. Depth is chromatic, focus is an outline, fills are flat or 18% veiled.

Don't reference a token across package boundaries at runtime. StyleX tokens are compile-time constants; a component that needs a token composes from its own layer instead of importing across the workspace boundary.

Don't let a browser default stand in for a designed control. Unstyled native form elements are the most visible defect the system can have, because they are the one surface the operator sees that the system did not draw.
